title: Interpreting learning dynamics of autoencoders: Transient scaling and emerging concepts of the Ising model
abstract: We study how unsupervised autoencoders trained on microscopic spin configurations from the Ising model learn macroscopic, theory-relevant variables underlying the data-generating process. Without embedding domain knowledge, we mimic a typical discovery setting: We quantify learning across multiple spatial (coarse-graining) scales and reveal two distinct dynamical regimes controlled by main hyperparameters (model depth, width, and learning rate) -- a magnetization-dominated regime and an energy-dominated regime characterized by trade-offs in their representation quality. The first regime is a transitory state exhibiting dynamical scaling and fluctuations that follow an ordering-to-scale; the second gradually shifts resolution towards smaller scales relevant for the energy representation. Deep models trained at moderate and fast rates become arrested before reaching these regimes. With a novel analysis of recursive-dynamic trajectories, we demonstrate that prediction errors induce flow fields that produce a common trajectory topology across all representation spaces. A dynamical viewpoint of learning is established in which intrinsic properties expose the effects of forced changes in representation during training. We utilize the intuition that learning operates as a process driven far from equilibrium by fluctuations from the training data and optimizer to provide an interpretive basis grounded in both the physical world and the machine models that represent it.
summary: This paper analyzes how autoencoders learn physical concepts from Ising model data by studying the dynamics of their training process. It identifies distinct dynamical regimes corresponding to magnetization and energy dominance within the latent space. The work establishes a theoretical framework viewing learning as a non-equilibrium process that reveals underlying topological structures.
main_problem: The study investigates how unsupervised autoencoders learn macroscopic, theory-relevant variables from microscopic spin configurations generated by the Ising model.
main_result: Learning dynamics reveal two distinct regimes (magnetization vs. energy dominated), and a common trajectory topology is found across representation spaces when analyzing prediction errors.
method: The authors analyze autoencoder training dynamics by studying how reconstruction loss drives trajectories in the low-dimensional latent space, using concepts from dynamical systems theory.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Ising model used to generate spin configurations. The machine learning model is a deterministic nonlinear autoencoder trained on these microscopic data sets.
key_observables: Learning dynamics, prediction errors inducing flow fields, magnetization ($M$), energy ($E$), and Spearman rank correlation between input differences and latent space distances.
important_parameters: Model depth/width, learning rate ($\lambda$), bottleneck size ($b$), and coarse-graining spatial scales.
main_assumptions: Learning is viewed as a process driven far from equilibrium by fluctuations; standard post hoc methods fail to capture the concept formation *process*.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how correlation between input differences ($\Delta M$ or $\Delta E$) and latent distance changes with bottleneck size, showing stability for magnetization topology in larger bottlenecks. Other figures track loss evolution across coarse-graining scales and show trajectories for $M$ and $E$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a dynamical viewpoint of learning by analyzing how autoencoders process Ising model data. It identifies two distinct training regimes (magnetization/energy) and uses recursive trajectory analysis to map the underlying topological structure preserved during compression.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, physics-grounded analogy for understanding feature extraction in deep learning, linking concepts like phase transitions or order parameters (magnetization/energy) directly to network dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Ising model spin configurations on a square lattice (left) are mapped to a binary representation (right). Spins pointing down (blue) are mapped to zero (white) and spins pointing up (red) to one (black). The two-dimensional binary representation is converted to floating-point numbers and flat- tened into a one-dimensional vector. This one-dimensional pixel vector serves as input to an autoencoder.

FIG. 2. Joint distribution of the entire dataset (black dots) over sample energy and magnetization. The area containing almost all samples from a given temperature is indicated by colored contours. At low temperatures, there are two distinct clusters with low energy and high absolute magnetization (upper and lower left). At high temperatures, a single cluster with a small absolute magnetization and higher energy becomes dominant (center-right).

FIG. 3. Auto-Encoder model architecture composed of an encoder (left) and decoder model (right). The encoder trans- forms the input with a sequence of linear and non-linear ReLU layers into a lower-dimensional latent representation, referred to as a bottleneck. The decoder transforms this latent rep- resentation with the same sequence of layers (but different parameters) into the output. The parameters of each lin- ear layer are optimized during training to reduce the mean squared deviation (MSD) between inputs and outputs.

FIG. 4. Validation loss evolution of raw data over training checkpoints averaged over all runs with the same model (depth, width, bottleneck) and learning rate. Each subplot shows the average across different seeds (seedmodel ∈{0, 1}, seedbatch ∈ {0, 1}) and batch sizes |B| ∈{30, 300, 3000} for a given model width and depth. The line styles correspond to different bottleneck sizes, while the line colors indicate the base learning rate used for training. All loss curves show a rapid initial decrease, followed by none or another rapid or slow decrease depending on the hyperparameters.
